newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Buyers to wait after USDA report.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Buyers to wait after USDA report.

text.p: Southeast Asian grains and oilseeds buyers said on Wednesday they will probably step back from the market to see if corn and soybean futures prices will drop to fresh lows after a bearish USDA report.

"I think December (corn prices in Chicago) will find its way to US$2.45 cents/bushel over the next few weeks, and buyers will be ready in a month...to import for first quarter or early second quarter" of 1997, one Indonesian trader said.
"U.S. weekly exports are looking very good but my guess is that as a whole prices will come under pressure," he added. "I hear this might be one of their largest harvests ever."

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Tuesday in its November crop report that the corn crop will reach 9.27 billion bushels, the third largest on record and three percent higher than its October estimate.
The soybean harvest was pegged at 2.40 billion bushels, the second largest crop ever, up two percent from last month.
Indonesian traders said a bigger crop in the United States could see local buyers stepping up imports, but added that they were likely to wait another month for Chicago prices to hit bottom.
While soybeans climbed above average trade estimates of 2.376 billion bushels, the USDA also raised its estimated usage by 35 million bushels.
"The supply might be larger. But demand also rose. I think buyers will have to make their decision soon," a Thai trader said.
But other dealers in Bangkok said the USDA report's impact on buying patterns may be limited.
Settasarn Settakarun, an advisor to Thai Cottonseed, Ricebran and Vegetable Oil Crushers Association, said soybean prices will not likely move in either direction.
"The current price level already reflected supply of around 2.3 billion bushels. I don't think the prices will move substantially in either direction," he said.

Another trader said: "I think at the moment, it's the local policy that affects buying. Buyers were sidelined awaiting the (Thai) Commerce Ministry to come up with concrete figures on soybean imports."

The Commerce Ministry, in an attempt to protect local farmers after elimination of import quotas for soybeans and soymeals, has asked for a commitment from animal feed producers and authorized importers to buy all local soybean products.
It also asked the industry to come up with its projection of demand for 1997 soon in order to set import-to-local product ratios.
Domestic prices in Southeast Asia were easier on the back of ample supplies, dealers said.
Indonesian corn was quoted at 405-410 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, down from 415-420 rupiah a week ago. Soymeal was unchanged at 800-810 rupiah/kg on sufficient stocks.
A trader from the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra said she has been seeing small arrivals at the start of the local harvest which has been putting pressure on prices.
"I have been getting 40 to 50 tonnes daily at the moment, but arrivals for the whole of Lampung will rise to between 1,000 and 2,000 tonnes in January," she said.
Thai soymeal prices fell further this week on rising supply.
Demand for 1996 was mostly covered with buyers focusing on purchases for next year, trade sources said.
Soymeal prices were quoted at around 9.60 baht a kg compared with 10.00 baht last week. Corn was at 4.36-4.40 baht a kg, up from 4.25-4.40 baht last week because of tighter supplies.
Traders expected prices of soymeal to dip further as more imported supplies came on the market.
There has been market talk that oil crushers might hold a tender for around 70,000 tonnes of soybeans in December.
In Malaysia, prices were unchanged from last week and were trending lower, dealers said.
They could not report any buying over the past week but generally agreed that demand could return by early/mid December.

"Everyone's covered for December up till the first quarter of next year," said a Singapore trader who tracks the Malaysian market. "If there is any buying, it should come in the next three weeks for February/March arrival."
Another dealer predicted that corn prices could fall another 10 ringgit in Malaysia next week in tandem with falling international prices.
"It has become a self-fulfilling prophecy for buyers these days when they decide not to buy and find the price falling accordingly next week," said the dealer.
Bulk corn ex-factory/godown in the central region was seen at 475 to 480 ringgit a tonne this week.

"A" grade wheat in bags was also quoted steady at 800 ringgit a tonne ex factory/godown in the central region while "local" wheat was trading at 500 to 510 ringgit. Soymeal was going for around 810 ringgit a tonne, same as last week.
